papers.title: SWE-Explore: Benchmarking How Coding Agents Explore Repositories

notes.takeaway: Isolates repository exploration as a standalone task: given an issue and a repo snapshot, an explorer returns a ranked list of line-level code regions under a fixed line budget, scored without writing or validating a patch.
notes.why: The repo-scale branch's distinction between reading a file and navigating a repository — SWE-Explore makes line-level navigation a measurable target across retrievers, search agents, and long-context selectors.

notes.takeaway: Across lexical/dense retrievers, general coding agents, and specialized localizers, agentic explorers form a clear tier above classical retrieval; file-level localization is already strong for modern methods, but line-level coverage and efficient ranking remain the axes separating state-of-the-art explorers.
notes.why: Direct evidence for the techniques ladder — where agentic navigation outperforms lexical/dense retrieval, and where the remaining headroom is (line-level precision, not file-level).

notes.takeaway: 848 issues across 10 programming languages and 203 repositories, with line-level ground truth distilled from independent successful agent trajectories (kept only when >=2 trajectories resolve the issue); a restricted-context downstream protocol confirms exploration metrics track repair success.
notes.why: The enterprise branch's polyglot-scale and evaluation-crisis concerns — trajectory-grounded supervision sidesteps contaminated or tautological ground truth, validated against actual repair.

papers.title: CORE-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Code Retrieval in the Era of Agentic Coding

notes.takeaway: Reframes code retrieval for agentic coding as requirement-driven repository search rather than query-to-snippet matching: real development requests carry a large intent-to-implementation gap, and the evidence needed for a change is scattered across code, configuration, dependencies, and docs instead of sitting in one function.
notes.why: Direct support for the foundations claim that code retrieval breaks classical text-IR assumptions — the vocabulary/intent mismatch and structurally-spread meaning show up here as a measurable benchmark gap that docstring-to-function tasks miss.

notes.takeaway: Each query is grounded in a concrete repository snapshot checked out to the commit immediately before its PR, and scoring rewards retrieving the multiple chunks an edit touches plus the broader context an agent browses — 632 repositories and 9.38M chunks at Level-2, with dense in-repository distractors.
notes.why: Operationalizes the repo-scale branch's 'a repository is a world you navigate': retrieval is measured over repository state with multi-target localization, the regime agent harnesses currently handle through iterative ls/grep/find rather than a single embedding lookup.

notes.takeaway: Embedding retrievers that score well on traditional code search collapse on the agentic levels — Qwen3-Embedding-8B falls from 71.7 NDCG@10 on Level-1 to 20.3 on Level-2 and 34.4 on Level-3 — and in-domain SFT on GitHub PR supervision helps across every difficulty regime but Recall@100 still drops as corpora grow denser and larger.
notes.why: Speaks to the enterprise branch's evaluation crisis: the benchmark builds temporally grounded, anti-leakage corpora (pre-PR checkout, LLM filtering of answer-leaking descriptions) and shows that standard code-search scores overstate a retriever's real usefulness to a coding agent.

papers.title: How Much Static Structure Do Code Agents Need? A Study of Deterministic Anchoring

notes.takeaway: Injecting offline-computed structural facts (call/inheritance/data-flow/config edges from PyCG plus AST extractors) as inline plain-text tags makes grep-first repository navigation deterministic: link-following rate rises from 0.15-0.18 to 0.21-0.24, run-to-run variance roughly halves, and trajectories shorten by 1.6 rounds. The right configuration is scale-dependent: medium repos (~35k LOC) favor bidirectional links, while large hub-heavy repos do better with inverse-only 'who-calls-me' edges that suppress high-degree helper noise.
notes.why: Concrete evidence for the repo-scale fork: instead of choosing retrieve-better-snippets versus query-a-code-graph, CodeAnchor folds a lightweight structured model back into the text view the agent already searches, and measures the navigation-versus-scale tradeoff that defines treating a repository as a world to traverse rather than a file to read.

notes.takeaway: Keeps lexical grep as the retrieval substrate and layers structure on top rather than replacing it: static call/inheritance topology yields +2.2pp Func@5 and +3.4pp Pass@1 on medium repos, while denser data-/config-flow tags saturate (+4.9 interaction rounds of overhead on Lite) and only pay off on the few implicit-dependency cases (3/274 Lite, 15/500 Verified), at roughly 10% more input tokens.
notes.why: Empirically instantiates the additive-ladder claim: lexical retrieval is retained for what it does well, structural/graph edges are added where behavior matters, and the diminishing returns of dense semantics show why each rung must be cost-justified rather than always-on.

papers.title: ProjAgent: Procedural Similarity Retrieval for Repository-Level Code Generation

notes.takeaway: ProjAgent adds procedural similarity as a retrieval signal alongside lexical and semantic ones: it represents a function's implementation behavior with LLM hidden-state projections, so it can retrieve helper functions that share a computational procedure (input validation, unit conversion, state transformation) even when names, types, and domain vocabulary differ. Its motivating pair of guard-clause validators scores only 0.38 BM25 and 0.59 embedding similarity, too low to surface. On REPOCOD ProjAgent reaches 41.14% Pass@1, and removing the procedural signal drops that to 25.76%, a larger fall than removing the semantic signal.
notes.why: This branch frames retrieval techniques as an additive ladder where each signal owns what the others miss; procedural similarity is a new rung capturing behavioral relatedness that lexical, dense, and dataflow signals do not, and the ablation shows it is complementary rather than redundant.

notes.takeaway: ProjAgent treats a repository as something to navigate: an agentic workflow decomposes the target function into reasoning steps, identifies and validates procedurally related functions per step, then expands the set with projection-similarity retrieval and merges it with lexical and semantic context to gather repository-specific APIs and symbols. A conservative static-analysis feedback loop then repairs the generated code against compiler and static-analysis output, adding a modest but measurable gain.
notes.why: This branch is about the repository as a world to traverse and the fork between retrieve-better-snippets and query-a-structured-model; ProjAgent sits on the retrieval side but adds behavior-level matching plus a static-analysis repair loop, showing repo-scale context assembly needs signals beyond surface similarity and a grounding check on the output.

papers.title: Agent Retrieval Bench: Evaluating Repository Context Retrieval for Coding Agents

notes.takeaway: The benchmark redefines the retrieval unit and the relevance target for repository scale: given a workflow-derived query and a repository frozen at its base commit, rank the files an agent needs to read next. Relevance is the next useful step in the software task, not query-to-file textual similarity, and the four positive tasks encode four different shapes of that indirection. code2test asks for the tests related to an implementation change, comment2context for context files beyond the reviewed file, trace2code for the root-cause source behind reproduced failure output rather than the visible test frames it mentions, and edit2ripple for the additional files a given anchored change touches. Interactive exploration does not remove the need to measure this layer, it only changes the cost model, and the logged trajectories show what that costs: an OpenAI strict-context agent reads 3.2 files per sample and Codex CLI recovered contexts show about 6 file/path events per sample, yet over the 287 code2test, comment2context and trace2code samples the agents never touch any gold file on 35.2% of OpenAI samples and 27.2 to 29.3% of Codex samples. Where gold is eventually reached, the median first hit is step 2 for OpenAI and step 3 for Codex.
notes.why: This branch treats a repository as a world to navigate rather than a file to read, and asks how the retrieve-better-snippets and query-a-structured-model camps relate with agentic navigation moving between them. The paper gives that navigation a measurable upstream surface: a third of agent trajectories never reach the file that mattered, which is a navigation failure that end-to-end patch scores absorb silently. Its own scope note is explicit that this is a component-level claim, not evidence that retrieval dominates patch failure.

notes.takeaway: No retrieval family dominates, and the reversals are the finding rather than the noise. Over all 345 positive samples Qwen3-Embedding-4B takes the best sample-weighted MRR, Qwen3-Embedding-8B the best Recall@20, and vectorless RepoMap the best Budgeted Context Yield at an 8k token budget, so the winner changes with the metric. Per-task winners diverge further: on trace2code, RepoMap leads on both MRR and Recall@20, plain lexical retrieval beats most embedding baselines on MRR, and Qwen3-4B posts a trace2code MRR of 0.0827 despite leading overall MRR. On edit2ripple the two Qwen model sizes swap order across context budgets, with 4B ahead at a fully packed 4k and 8B ahead at a fully packed 8k. Lexical matching stays competitive with RepoMap on MRR and BCY while neither beats the embedding models on Recall@20. Budgeted Context Yield is the metric that makes this legible, asking how much labeled gold context actually fits inside a fixed token budget after a ranker has ordered files, rather than scoring rank position in the abstract.
notes.why: This branch models techniques as an additive ladder where lexical owns rare tokens, dense embeddings own intent, structural methods own behavior, and cascades place each where its cost is justified. The results are a direct measurement of that additivity: the trace2code case, where a failure trace names a test file while the root cause is an implementation file that looks nothing like the error text, is the paper's strongest evidence that semantic embeddings alone are insufficient, and the budget-dependent size reversal shows the choice is a cascade-placement decision rather than a leaderboard.

notes.takeaway: The construction spends most of its effort on the hygiene that repository-scale evaluation usually lacks. The 427 samples span 25 repositories and are evaluated against frozen base-commit corpora using pre-resolution files only, so the fixed code cannot leak; the combined corpus manifest covers 308 base-commit snapshots, 392K files and 7.9M chunks, with the released samples drawing on 271 snapshots. Validity diagnostics report complete corpus coverage, zero schema or corpus invalid rows, and zero fatal shortcut leakage from exact gold paths, raw patches, fix commits or autogenerated review artifacts. A fifth subset targets abstention rather than recall, pairing 50 natural evidence-backed no-gold cases with 32 counterfactual wrong-repository controls, and it exposes a calibration gap: selective thresholds look useful when the counterfactual controls are mixed in, but fail to improve selective success on the 50 natural no-gold cases. A 45-sample single-run closed-tool seed-intervention pilot finds retrieval-derived initial context yields higher File F1 with less post-seed exploration than random non-gold context, while oracle gold context still leaves substantial headroom.
notes.why: This branch holds that scale changes which problems exist, and names an evaluation crisis where ground truth is contaminated or tautological. This benchmark is a worked answer to that specific charge, with base-commit freezing against fixed-code leakage, an audited leakage sweep over the obvious shortcut channels, and a no-gold subset that separates knowing when to abstain from knowing what to rank. That the abstention thresholds hold up only against the easy counterfactual controls is the more useful result, because the wrong-repository case is not the one a production agent faces.

papers.title: VITAL-RAG: Invariance Race for Context Allocation in Coding Agents

notes.takeaway: The paper isolates a stage neither the better-snippets camp nor the code-graph camp owns: what happens after ranking and before generation, when retrieved views compete for a bounded model input. Measured over 16,490 screened RepoBench tasks from 2,798 repositories (8,556 Java, 7,934 Python), required cross-file evidence enters the selected top five for 64.16% of tasks but survives intact inside a 4,096-token input for only 39.59% — a gap of 24.57 points, 26.37 on Java and 22.64 on Python. Recall@4K credits only a complete labeled snippet, so a surviving path or a clipped signature does not count. The cause is authority multiplication: a repository index renders one code object as a signature, a body slice, a call site and a test fragment, and when each competes independently, one object claims several input positions and clips the independent helper the task actually needs. VITAL-RAG closes most of the gap by quotienting that authority, raising Recall@4K from 39.59% to 63.67% while using 35.63% fewer evidence tokens, without changing the candidate set.
notes.why: This branch treats a repository as a world to navigate rather than a file to read. The paper adds a consequence specific to that scale: at repository scale the same object exists in several renderings, so the count of representations rather than the relevance of objects ends up deciding context share. That makes retrieval-side metrics misleading on their own. The paper shows a context builder can raise input-level recall by 24 points with the ranking held fixed, and conversely that improving Recall@5 buys nothing when the evidence is clipped during rendering — so anyone measuring repository navigation with recall at k is measuring the wrong end of the pipeline.

notes.takeaway: VITAL-RAG is a retriever-agnostic allocation layer rather than another rung on the lexical/dense/graph ladder. It accepts ranked multi-view evidence from sparse, dense or graph retrieval and takes object identity from a provenance adapter supplied by the repository index, which can be parser-qualified symbol IDs, graph nodes, or in their evaluation the pair of normalized path and casefolded identifier. Allocation runs in three stages. Views mapping to the same canonical object compete for one position; the strongest by retrieval order takes it and inherits its score, with no accumulation across views, and an object's authority multiplicity is formally capped at one, so adding renderings may replace an object's representative but cannot buy it a second slot. One of the five positions is reserved for a query-relevant companion, admitted only if it sits on a source path already represented in the core set and shares identifier-like tokens with the task, which preserves the validator or exception helper that pure object-level invariance would erase. Rendering then assigns per-object and global token budgets, taking the largest line-complete rendering that fits. The controls this replaces do not work: exact deduplication moves Recall@4K by 0.02 points, and Canonical-5, File Quota, MMR and Entity-First 4+1 all reach roughly 64% Recall@5 and about 4.42 canonical objects among five candidates while landing between 39.41% and 39.59% at 4K.
notes.why: This branch reads the field as an additive ladder where cascades put each technique where its cost is justified. This contribution is orthogonal to the ladder and worth separating from it: allocation is a distinct decision from retrieval, it is settled by provenance rather than text similarity, and the familiar diversity knobs are the wrong instrument for it. The control table is the useful evidence — four standard redundancy and coverage methods, each removing a different kind of repetition, all landing within 0.2 points of each other at the model input. That says the bottleneck is not diversity at all, but who owns a slot and how much text they get.

papers.title: PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks

notes.takeaway: PaiChecker treats misalignment detection as a semantic comparison over textual artifacts first and code second, on the argument that intent read off a diff is ambiguous when the intended behavior spans hundreds or thousands of lines, while PR descriptions and discussions summarize changes at the same abstraction level as issues. Phase I runs three specialized subagents, each over a focused artifact subset with its own workflow; Phase II has a coordinator synthesize cross-subagent evidence to catch misalignments outside the taxonomy and re-verify each label against its own textual reasoning; Phase III validates the label against the code. On SWE-Gym it reaches 92.12% binary accuracy and 84.66% exact match, beating the strongest of three prompting and four agent-framework baselines by 5.13-12.39 accuracy points and 9.02-17.76 exact-match points, and 91.67% on SWE-bench Multilingual, holding across GPT-5.3 Codex, Qwen-3.5 Plus, Gemini-3.1-Pro Preview and Claude-Sonnet-4.6 backbones.
notes.why: This branch names an evaluation crisis where ground truth is contaminated or tautological. Here that crisis has a number and a scrubber. The same PR-to-issue pipeline also builds training sets for code LLMs and software agents, so a misaligned pair is not merely a bad test case, it is supervision teaching a model to produce incomplete, unrelated, or defective patches. A checker that runs at construction time is the difference between a corpus that can be grown and one that degrades as it scales.

papers.title: Change2Task: From Repository Changes to Executable Coding Agent Tasks and Environments

notes.takeaway: The paper's framing is that executable environments, not task ideas, are the scarce resource. It cites daVinci-Env at 45,320 Docker environments across more than 12.8K repositories for roughly $891K in construction cost, and SWE-Universe at 807,693 verifiable environments on specialized distributed infrastructure, with per-task snapshots further multiplying images, storage, registry traffic and cold starts. Change2Task sits downstream of the setup problem EnvBench, SetupBench, Repo2Run and RepoLaunch attack: it starts once a base is runnable and asks how many verified, developer-grounded tasks one prepared base can carry. Reusing 388 modern bases cuts environment time 58.4%, storage 71.2% and end-to-end expenditure 10.8%. Construction escalates only as repository drift demands it - Level 1 reverses the source patch when it still applies, Level 2 locates the historical post-change block in the modern file and swaps in its reindented pre-change form under the same scope and executable gates, and Level 3 hands PR evidence and modern context to a construction agent for at most four attempts, ranking survivors by source change profile fidelity and edit complexity.
notes.why: Enterprise-scale code work hits build complexity and a contaminated evaluation base at the same time, and this addresses both with one move. Binding a task to its original historical revision is what makes a benchmark go stale and what forces a fresh environment per task; rebuilding the same maintenance event on a maintained head keeps the developer's intent while inheriting a working build. The three-level escalation doubles as a measurement of repository drift itself - which historical changes still replay verbatim, which need structural mapping, and which need a model to reconstruct at all.

papers.title: OwlPath: Lossless Knowledge Compression for LLM Bug Repair

notes.takeaway: OwlPath projects a tree-sitter code graph into an OWL2 ontology and answers structural queries with SPARQL 1.1 property paths. Every edge maps to one axiom: extends becomes rdfs:subClassOf, implements, calls and imports become transitive object properties, contains stays non-transitive, and the projection is a bijection, one axiom per source tuple, which is the sense in which nothing structural is lost. The payoff is complexity: the transitive closure materializes once at O(n+m) and serves from cache at O(1) amortized, against a recursive SQL CTE at O(n^k) for k hops - 4.7 measured minutes of single-threaded extract-and-project on a 1.4M-symbol repository. On 18 matched SWE-bench Pro instances holding agent (Hermes), model (DeepSeek-V4-Flash), 70-turn cap and prompt template constant, strict-apply is comparable at 68.4% against 66.7%, while tokens fall 28.8% (1,416K vs 1,989K) and wall clock 39.5% (648s vs 1,071s). Offline on 67 instances the separation is larger: recall 0.464 against 0.226 for string-match codegraph and an 88.1% hit rate against 59.7%; on a 37-question structural benchmark recall@all rises from 4.4% to 28.8%, scoring 69-80% on transitive-caller and interface-implementation questions.
notes.why: The branch's claim is that the ladder is additive and graph methods own behavior - the queries whose answer is structurally connected to the question but shares no string with it: a subclass chain, a transitive caller path, an interface hierarchy. This measures that case cleanly, and what moves is retrieval quality and cost, not the repair rate. It also supplies the cascade's cost discipline in an unusually direct experiment: forcing the knowledge-map advisory and closure results into every prompt doubles token consumption, 2,835K against 1,416K, and leaves strict-apply flat at 68.8% versus 68.4%, while keeping the tool optional buys the same success for half the tokens.

notes.takeaway: The setup is the repository-scale bind stated as arithmetic: roughly 100K tokens of context against a repository of millions of lines, so the agent must retrieve a structurally relevant subset before it can reason about the bug at all. OwlPath sits on the query-a-structured-model side of the fork but adds an orientation aid for the first move. The OWL Software Knowledge Map is a 3KB summary emitted once, on the agent's first search call, in two layers: a module directory tree with each module scored log(symbols)*0.5 + log(files)*0.3 + log(symbols per file)*0.2, and an issue map built from 4-8 identifiers extracted from the problem statement and test patch, each resolved to candidate symbols. The stated aim is compressing the initial search space from thousands of files to one advisory, replacing a baseline loop of grep, read, grep, read over five to ten iterations. Evaluation seals each repository's git history first - branches and tags deleted, reflogs expired, gc prune - so the agent cannot recover the gold fix from history.
notes.why: The fork this branch names is between retrieving better snippets and querying a structured model of the repository, with agentic navigation walking between them. OwlPath is a clean instance of the second that leaves the agent in charge of when to walk, since closure is opt-in per query rather than always-on context. The 3KB map is the more portable idea in it: the expensive failure at repository scale is rarely a bad ranking, it is spending the first several turns in the wrong module, and a one-time orientation is cheap insurance against that.

papers.title: Agentic Method for Deterministic Validation of Legacy Code Migration

notes.takeaway: American Express reports a validation loop for COBOL-to-Java migration that answers the ground-truth problem by refusing to author ground truth at all: the legacy program is the oracle. Both the COBOL source and the generated Java target are instrumented with mocks and run off-mainframe on commodity hardware, and a Parity Gate executes both on the same witness inputs and reports end-state discrepancies across three equivalence axes. A test case is accepted only if it increases branch coverage and both systems agree; a case that reaches a new branch but diverges between COBOL and Java is rejected. The authors first establish that input search alone is not enough: combinatorial interaction testing, adaptive random testing, search-based generation and its many-objective variants, fuzzing, and MAP-Elites all converge to similar coverage ceilings, which tells them the remaining branches are structurally unreachable without changing state that lives outside the input space. The Locksmith Loop runs Witness Search with six algorithms until two consecutive sweeps find no new branches, has a deterministic analyzer identify the Locked Paragraph blocking further exploration, has a supervisory Authoring Layer propose a parity-preserving mutation to both targets, then resumes search from the newly reachable region. Across three programs of 430 to 4,114 source lines it reaches near-complete coverage on two open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on an internal production-like one; on the production-shape run, 135 of 142 paragraphs (95.1%) and 101 of 146 static transitions (69.2%) from 166 test cases, with mutation contributing 47 of those transitions against 54 from search alone.
notes.why: This branch holds that enterprise scale changes which problems exist, and legacy is where that is most literal: the specification is gone, the behavior includes decades of broken-as-usual cases that became the product definition by accident, and the test data covers a handful of real scenarios with a long tail untested. The evaluation crisis the branch names, ground truth that is contaminated or tautological, is resolved here by differential execution rather than by better annotation, and that is the transferable move for any migration where 1:1 behavioral equivalence is feasible, which the authors extend to Java-to-Kotlin, C#-to-Java and C-to-Go. Worth carrying over as well is the honesty about the proxy: they state that branch coverage is an imperfect predictor of fault detection, anchor acceptance on parity instead of coverage, and decline to claim the resulting suite is sufficient for migration sign-off on its own.

papers.title: MRCoder: An Efficient Context Selecting Approach for Repository-Level Code Generation

notes.takeaway: MRCoder attacks the recall-precision trap that repository-scale RAG walks into. Their motivating measurement, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on CoderEval with BM25, shows Pass@1 rising with Top-K and then falling while precision drops monotonically and both token count and latency climb: past a point, retrieving more of the repository makes the model worse and slower at once. The fix does not build a code graph and does not iterate retrieval. It writes a draft first. In the Map phase the retrieved blocks are partitioned into groups, each group is paired with the target query, and a lightweight draft model generates draft code per group independently. Structure-Aware Draft-Guided Selection then scores candidate contexts against those drafts from two perspectives: API consistency, using the call relationships in the draft to keep repository-specific APIs the implementation is likely to invoke plus reference patterns for external API usage, and logical similarity between draft and candidate. The Reduce phase aggregates the surviving contexts for final generation, with parallel verification accelerating decoding. On CoderEval and DevEval with Qwen2.5-Coder and DeepSeek-Coder backbones, accuracy improves over strong baselines while tokens fall 30-50% and inference time falls up to 52.1% on CoderEval and 48.6% on DevEval.
notes.why: This branch frames repository scale as a fork between retrieving better snippets and querying a structured model, and MRCoder is a third position worth naming: use a cheap generation to discover which structural relations matter, then select on them. The draft functions as a query rewrite in the target language, so API-call structure becomes usable as a relevance signal without an index or a graph over the repository. The comparison against the alternatives is the practically useful part. RepoFormer-style control tokens decide whether to retrieve but leave retrieval noise intact, and LongCodeZip's perplexity-based line selection needs multiple forward passes and pays for it in latency, so a method that improves quality and cost together is the exception rather than the norm here.

notes.takeaway: The efficiency result is a cascade result. The expensive backbone never sees the raw candidate pool: a lightweight draft model runs first over partitioned groups in parallel, and its output is used only as a selection signal, not as the answer. Selection itself is structural rather than neural scoring, matching draft against candidate on API call relationships and logical similarity, so the second stage is cheap too. Only the filtered context reaches the backbone, and parallel verification then attacks autoregressive decoding latency directly. Measured against the RAG baseline the cascade cuts tokens 30-50% and inference time up to 52.1% for Qwen2.5-Coder and 38.0% for DeepSeek-Coder at k=3 on CoderEval, with 48.6% and 39.0% on DevEval, while raising accuracy. The contrast case in the paper is instructive: RepoFormer reaches the lowest token consumption of any method by aggressively deciding not to retrieve at all, needing only one token of inference, and pays for it in accuracy.
notes.why: The branch's claim is that a cascade earns its place by putting each technique where its cost is justified, and this is a clean instance with the cost accounted on both axes. The generalizable pattern is that a draft from a small model is a better query than the original request, because it is expressed in the vocabulary of the code being written rather than the vocabulary of the request, which is the query-code mismatch this explorer opens with. The RepoFormer comparison marks the boundary: skipping retrieval is always the cheapest option and the cost axis alone will always prefer it, so a cascade has to be judged on both numbers at once.

papers.title: Scrouting: Cost-Aware Routing of Coding Agents by Scouting the Repository First

notes.takeaway: A trained 7B searcher, not a retrieval index, is the navigation layer here. SuperScout-7B is Qwen2.5-Coder-7B fine-tuned with LoRA on a single GPU over 19,905 search trajectories sliced from openly licensed agent traces, each ending in a synthesized handoff-emission turn where the file list is extracted deterministically from the trace and the reproduction record copied verbatim, with only free-form notes model-written. Traces are success-filtered against the gold patch and deduplicated to two per issue so the corpus counts distinct bugs. The handoff it emits is a structured, deliberately short artifact: implicated files with line regions ranked by confidence, a reproduction attempt naming file, command, and observed output, dead ends already tried, and repository notes. Two findings about the searcher stand out. Decoding dominates training: greedy decoding finds the right files at 0.110 while a single sampled draw at temperature 0.9 reaches 0.306, because sampling raises the searcher's willingness to commit to a handoff from 0.213 to 0.718 at an 18% cost in per-handoff recall. And localization transfers across languages it never saw -- file-level F1 of 0.630 on six untrained languages against 0.455 on the three trained ones.
notes.why: The branch's fork is between retrieving better snippets and querying a structured model of the repository, with agentic navigation walking between them, and this is the agentic lane made cheap enough to run on every task. The design choice worth arguing with is that the navigation product is a document rather than a set of retrieved chunks: files with line regions, a runnable reproduction, and an explicit list of dead ends, sized at about a page so it fits in front of any downstream fixer. Prior small localizers train comparable models but terminate in one predetermined consumer; here the artifact is portable across a four-model pool. The decoding result is the practical warning for anyone deploying a small navigator: the failure mode was not that the model could not find files but that greedy decoding made it reluctant to declare a result, and the fix was an inference setting, not more training. Contamination control is handled at the corpus level with a 23-repository blocklist covering all 11 SWE-bench Pro repositories and 12 Verified ones, verified by a programmatic gate -- which is what makes the cross-language transfer claim readable at all.

notes.takeaway: The verify-then-strip gate is the paper's answer to a scout that hallucinates. Before any fixer sees the handoff, a sandbox replays the claimed reproduction command against the unpatched repository; if the command does not genuinely fail, both the claim and its generated test file are removed, and if it does, the test is materialized so the fixer can run it directly. Calibration found that most of the searcher's reproduction claims are in fact false, so the gate is load-bearing rather than a safety flourish -- without it the handoff would inject confident, wrong context into every downstream attempt. Injection is blanket: whichever fixer is selected receives the surviving handoff identically, and when no handoff is produced at all the fixer proceeds from the issue text alone, which defines the system's floor as fixer-solo performance. The whole trajectory is a single pass, with no parallel sampling and no mid-task escalation between models.
notes.why: The branch's framing is that the bottleneck has moved from model capability to the infrastructure problem of putting fresh, authorized, build-grounded context in front of an agent, and this is a concrete instance: the context is grounded by execution in a sandbox at the moment it is assembled, and anything that fails to reproduce is deleted rather than downweighted. That is a stronger contract than confidence scoring, and it is worth contrasting with concurrent escalation-based routers, which restart the strong model from scratch and throw away the cheap model's evidence at exactly the moment it becomes expensive to recompute. The measured payoff supports the framing over the routing story: the handoff is what moves the numbers, and it moves them by lifting cheaper fixers toward the frontier rather than by raising the ceiling. The open question the paper leaves is scope -- verification here covers reproduction claims only, while implicated files and notes pass through unverified, so the gate proves the one part of the handoff that happens to be executable.

papers.title: DeepRepoQA: Code Repository Question Answering with Deep Agent Exploration

notes.takeaway: Repository question answering is posed as planning rather than retrieval. DeepRepoQA builds a Monte-Carlo search tree over the repository and runs four agents per node: Perception writes a situational report from the node's own trajectory and its siblings' attempts, so planning can avoid repeated trials without storing full sibling transcripts; Planning proposes the next action; Execution runs it and filters the raw result into curated evidence; Evaluation assigns a scalar value. Simulation is a single agent step rather than a multi-step rollout, with the evaluation output directly setting Q(s,a), and selection uses UCT with at most three children per node over 15 iterations. Evidence accumulates on the root-to-node memory path that structures the prompt, and the synthesized answer must cite at least one supporting code span. Ablations put the weight on the search machinery: removing MCTS costs 2.27 overall points, removing the Perception Agent 1.73, and removing the Evaluation Agent 3.50.
notes.why: This branch's split is between retrieving better snippets and navigating a repository as a structured world. DeepRepoQA is the navigation side taken to its conclusion, and its stated motivation is the specific failure of single-path ReAct agents: evidence lying outside the chosen trajectory is simply missed, so exploration has to branch and be scored. On SWE-QA, expanded here to 15 repositories and 720 question-answer pairs, that buys up to 7.08 points over SWE-agent on Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct.

notes.takeaway: The action space is a deliberate layering rather than a single retrieval method. Tree-sitter ASTs back index-based lookup through FindClass, FindFunction and FindCodeSnippet, which locate classes, functions and snippets precisely without relying on fuzzy or semantic search; SemanticSearch runs over chunk embeddings for intent-shaped queries; ViewCode inspects specific spans. The RAG baselines it displaces are the standard ones: sliding-window chunks of 500 lines with 50-line overlap, and function- or class-level chunks, both indexed with voyage-code-3 and retrieved top-10. The ablation is where this gets interesting: removing semantic search costs 1.07 overall points, the smallest drop of the four components tested, while removing the Evaluation Agent costs 3.50.
notes.why: This branch treats lexical, dense and structural methods as an additive ladder and asks where each rung's cost is justified. DeepRepoQA puts a number on one version of that question: with precise structural lookup available and a scored search policy on top, the dense-retrieval rung contributes least. What carries the gain is deciding where to look next and judging what came back, not how the individual lookup is implemented.

sections.label: Why Code != Text IR
sections.summary: Code retrieval is not text IR with a different corpus: query/code vocabulary mismatch, an open code lexicon, and meaning that lives in structure all break the assumptions of classical IR.
themes: Vocabulary mismatch: a developer's query and the target snippet often share almost no tokens (CodeSearchNet).
Open vocabulary: code coins identifiers endlessly, so OOV cripples neural LMs (Big Code != Big Vocabulary).
Structure is signal text IR throws away: data/control flow, call graphs (MISIM, GraphCodeBERT).
The intent→query→code chain is lossy at every hop, spawning a whole query-reformulation subfield.
Even metrics can't be borrowed: CodeBLEU re-injects AST + data flow that BLEU and exact-match miss.
Industry consensus: 'mgrep finds the file, grep finds the line' — no single mode suffices, everyone ends up hybrid.
gaps: Cross-paper retrieval scores (MRR on CodeSearchNet) are not apples-to-apples; preprocessing and language subsets differ — the fragmentation CoIR was built to fix.
Pre-2016 classic lexical/structural search (Sourcerer, Portfolio, Sniff, grep/ctags) is absent (pre-arXiv venues).

sections.label: Techniques: Lexical/Neural/Graph
sections.summary: An additive ladder, not a sequence of replacements: lexical owns rare tokens, dense embeddings own intent, graph methods own behavior, and cascades place each technique where its cost is justified.
themes: Rung 1 — lexical/trigram/BM25: fast, exact, interpretable, owns rare-token recall (Zoekt lineage, CodeMatcher).
Rung 2 — neural bi-encoders + contrastive learning: CodeBERT, ContraCode, CoCoSoDa; need hard negatives (RocketQA) or they underperform.
Rung 3 — AST/graph: data flow (GraphCodeBERT), flow graphs (deGraphCS), GNNs (GraphSearchNet), graph matching.
Rung 4 — hybrid retrieve-then-rerank / late interaction: multi-stage ranking (Lin et al.), ColBERT, Cascaded Fast & Slow, CoRNStack.
Fuse on ranks, not scores: BM25 and dense lanes live on incomparable scales; RRF sidesteps calibration.
Contriever is the receipt: unsupervised dense loses to BM25 — dense only wins with supervision.
gaps: Dense/ANN index was down during gathering — recall is lexical/hybrid only; CoRNStack metrics unverified via live lookup.
Graph methods are most expressive but cost parsing + GNN inference, hard to amortize across a multi-million-file monorepo.

sections.label: Repository-Scale & Code Graphs
sections.summary: A file is a unit you read; a repository is a world you navigate. The field forks into retrieve-better-snippets (iterated similarity RAG) versus query-a-structured-model (code graphs), with agentic navigation walking between them.
themes: Camp 1 — similarity, iterated: RepoCoder's retrieve-generate-retrieve loop; DraCo steers it with dataflow.
Camp 2 — query a structured world model: CodexGraph (graph DB + LLM-written queries), CodeGRAG (GNN expert), AOCI (symbolic-semantic blueprint).
Code-property-graph / knowledge-graph lineage: QVoG at 1M+ LOC, Code Digital Twin for tacit knowledge.
Camp 3 — agentic navigation: SWE-agent's agent-computer interface, OpenHands, MAGIS, LocAgent, CodePlan, ARISE.
Localization is a first-class sub-problem; flat similarity misses fix sites several call/import hops from the symptom.
Retrieval scope is three problems: local-aware, global-aware, third-party-library-aware (A^3-CodGen).
gaps: Graphs cost a static-analysis build step + language-specific extractors + index maintenance; similarity RAG is cheaper and language-agnostic.
Referenced-but-uncorpus: RepoGraph (ICLR 2025), GRACE multi-semantic code graphs (arXiv:2509.05980) — the next reading.
Many results are small-N arXiv preprints (Jin n=24 localization tasks; AOCI industrial slice n=19).

sections.label: Enterprise Codebase Challenges
sections.summary: Scale does not just make existing problems bigger — it changes which problems exist: billions of LOC, polyglot dependency chains, access boundaries, dead code, tribal knowledge, build complexity, and an evaluation crisis where ground truth is contaminated or tautological.
themes: Sheer size: Google ~2B LOC, 9M files, ~40K commits/day — query-time linear search is infeasible.
Escalation ladder: grep → trigram (Zoekt) → semantic index (Kythe) → incremental build-integrated (Glean) → cross-repo precise nav (SCIP). Text layer and semantic layer are routinely conflated.
Polyglot: defects hide at the language boundary; dependency-usage context (K-Trans) carries the hard-to-retrieve knowledge.
Tribal/proprietary knowledge: the 'why' lives in a person or Slack thread; product context lifts decision compliance 46%→95%.
Access-control boundaries: 'find references' that returns unreadable code is a leak — the thinnest academic sub-topic.

Local benchmark projects encode the real enterprise tasks: EnterpriseBench (multi-repo nav, tool-access-as-variable, dead_code_necropsy), CodeScaleBench (benchmarks the retrieval engines, not just LLMs), codeprobe (contamination-proof probes, multi-source consensus).
gaps: Access-control / retrieval-under-permission-boundaries is near-absent academically (only published EnterpriseBench + Sourcegraph compliance framing).
Industrial systems (Kythe/Zoekt/Glean/SCIP) are blog-grounded, not peer-reviewed.
Benchmark numbers collapse on production: Passerine reached ~73% plausible on machine-reported but only ~25.6% plausible / 17.9% correct on human-reported Google bugs.

sections.label: Frontier & Open Problems
sections.summary: The bottleneck is no longer 'can a model write a function' but an infrastructure problem: put fresh, authorized, dependency-correct, build-grounded context in front of an agent inside a living monorepo.
themes: Staleness-aware retrieval: stale context is net-negative — gate retrieval on freshness, not just relevance (Weng; DocSync).
Incremental real-time indexing: reframe indexing cost from O(repository) to O(changes) (Glean) — almost no peer-reviewed work, industry holds the frontier.
Graph-guided edit localization: 69.7% of correctly localized bugs need multi-hop KG traversal (KGCompass); GALA extends to multimodal GUI bugs.
Symbolic+semantic fusion at monorepo scale: nobody ships the fused, always-fresh index — the unclaimed prize (AOCI, QVoG vs Kythe/SCIP/Zoekt/Glean).
Access-control & tribal-knowledge retrieval: 'bounded delegation' with least-privilege scoping is what 860 developers asked for (To Copilot and Beyond).
Honest evaluation: contamination (Riddell) and tool-vs-no-tool causality undermine benchmark numbers unless explicitly controlled.
gaps: Permission-aware retrieval and tribal-knowledge retrieval are the thinnest academically; enforcement leans on industry (PermLLM arXiv:2505.22860, Access Control for LLM Agents arXiv:2510.11108).
Long-context-vs-retrieval policy is genuinely open and thin in this corpus (Gemini 1.5 long-context referenced but absent); RepoQA is the needle-in-haystack foil.
Incremental indexing has almost no peer-reviewed coverage.

Make permission a first-class retrieval feature, not a post-hoc filter: 'find references' must respect what the caller is allowed to read, or it leaks. The thinnest academic sub-topic; enforcement leans on PermLLM-style permissioned LLMs and dynamic ACLs for agentic information flows.
Contamination-proof eval from private history

Public benchmarks (HumanEval, SWE-bench) are memorized; Riddell quantifies the seen-subset advantage. Mine contamination-proof probes from private/own repo history (codeprobe) instead of trusting memorized public sets.
Symbolic+semantic hybrid index at monorepo scale

Symbolic indexes (Kythe/SCIP) are precise but build-coupled; semantic embeddings are cheap but imprecise on exact references. Nobody ships the fused, always-fresh index — the unclaimed prize (AOCI, QVoG are the corpus anchors).
Staleness-aware retrieval

Carry commit timestamps / version pins into the index and decline stale context rather than serving it — Weng shows serving stale context is worse than serving nothing (obsolete-API refs in 15/17 samples).
Polyglot dependency-aware retrieval

Cross-language defects hide at the boundary; retrieving class definitions plus their dependencies is vital for code buildability (K-Trans: dependency-usage examples contribute most; Multilingual Code Intelligence survey).
Tribal-knowledge retrieval

The 'why' of a decision lives in people, Slack threads, design docs — never in source. A separate retrieval substrate for decisions/specs/personas lifted compliance 46%→95%; it is retrievable and measurably changes behavior.
Build-graph-grounded context selection
What even is the dependency graph is a question the build system answers; ground context selection in the build graph (Kythe/Glean are build-integrated) rather than text similarity over files.
Tool-vs-no-tool causal evaluation

The field lacks a clean isolation of 'did the tool help, or did the model already know?' Always report a no-tool baseline and isolate the tool variable (CodeScaleBench engines comparison; codeprobe MCP-vs-no-MCP isolation modes).
Long-context vs retrieval policy

When does a million-token full-repo dump beat selective retrieval? Capacity is not comprehension (RepoQA); a <5%-of-window grounded plan rivals full-repo GPT-4o (MutaGReP). The honest open question is the crossover point.
Incremental real-time index maintenance
Reframe indexing from O(repository) to O(changes): a 40K-commits/day monorepo cannot be fully re-indexed per change. Glean is the production exemplar; peer-reviewed work is nearly absent.
Graph-guided edit localization

Flat similarity structurally misses bug-fix sites: 69.7% of correctly localized bugs needed multi-hop KG traversal (KGCompass). Build a language-agnostic, incrementally-updatable repository graph before scaling embeddings.
Cost-latency-bounded retrieval at scale

Latency and UX are first-order at enterprise scale (Meta CodeCompose). Design retrieval under explicit cost/latency budgets — a cascade that spends the expensive technique only on a short pre-pruned list.
